judged.reasons: X is the stronger essay for an admissions reader because it has a real arc. The phone problem is set up early ("What I could not do, for years, was answer the phone"), the payoff comes late ("Last month the shop phone rang... 'Carvalho Shoe Service.' It took three tries"), and it closes by linking the shop to her grandmother: "My avó is still working on mine. I'll wait for her, too." That echo of the man who waited is good structure. The cost is that X leans on familiar AI-essay moves, and some of the glue is made up: "The shop taught me a different kind of listening," "People tell you a lot without saying a word, if you know where to look," "That mattered more than I expected," the overwritten "the word that belonged to me came out of my own mouth instead of being traded for a safer one," and an invented origin story ("Sitting across from her, I started wondering how the brain gets words back"). Y sounds more like Inês: it opens on "Hi, shoe repair." and uses "I hate the phone," "the 'shoe repair' thing," and the self-correction "I have never once answered the shop phone with the name. Actually, that stopped being true last month," which fits the note that she corrects herself. Its deadpan ending, "He was calling to ask if we fix purses. We don't.", is braver than X's tidy bow. But Y is mostly the interview notes reordered. Paragraphs start like catalog entries ("I work there on Saturdays," "The thing I'm weirdly good at is heels," which echoes the interview question). The dad's quote ("The shop isn't a person, it doesn't need anyone") is never followed up, the essay offers almost no reflection, and the "(sample essay for a fictional student)" label is a production artifact. Overall: Y is more faithful to the notes and more human in its wording; X is better built and more persuasive, but adds feelings and lessons that are not in the notes.
